The View from SomewherePart III · Surveys that overlap

Chapter 13

More than two answers

Web edition. Figure 13.3 is live: set the two distributions, or a drift, and watch the forbidden cells and the quantile coupling.

Here is an invented case. Two surveys of one city ask the same question about the local schools, with four possible answers, which I number 1 to 4 from poor to excellent. In the first survey the answers are distributed as p=(0.40, 0.10, 0.40, 0.10), a lumpy distribution that I chose on purpose. The second survey was run by a warmer interviewer. Of everyone who would have said 1, 2 or 3, 40 percent said the next answer up instead, and nothing else differs. The second survey’s answers are then distributed as q=(0.24, 0.22, 0.28, 0.26). Chapter 11 gave you the rule that contextuality-by-default applies in such a case. Do not pool the two copies of the question. Treat them as two variables and ask whether they can be coupled, together with everything else in the system, so that they agree as often as their margins allow. With two possible answers that instruction picks out a single coupling. With four it picks out a family, and the family is where this chapter lives.

Two versions of the rule are in the literature, and they disagree about this very example. Under one, the two copies of the school question are already contextual by themselves, before any third survey closes a loop. Under the other, two copies of one question can never be contextual by themselves. Which version one adopts changes what a loop test says about real surveys, and three of our research cycles were spent finding out how much. By the end of the chapter you will be able to say which splits of the answers each version requires, why the first version fails the example, and what the second version pays for its silence.

13.1Agreeing as often as possible, with four answers

A coupling of the two copies is a four-by-four table r with row sums p and column sums q. Entry rij is how often copy 1 gives answer i while copy 2 gives answer j. The set of such tables is the transportation polytope of p and q; for four answers it has dimension nine. The probability that the copies agree is the trace of r, and it cannot exceed ∑imin(pi,qi), because rii≤min(pi,qi). In the example that ceiling is 0.24+0.10+0.28+0.10=0.72. A coupling is maximal when its diagonal sits at the ceiling.

Maximal does not mean unique. Fix the diagonal at (0.24,0.10,0.28,0.10) and see what is left. Answer 1 has 0.16 of its mass to place off the diagonal and answer 3 has 0.12; answers 2 and 4 are used up. Column 2 still needs 0.12 and column 4 needs 0.16. Nothing is needed in columns 1 and 3, so the off-diagonal mass can only go from rows 1 and 3 to columns 2 and 4. Send x from row 1 to column 2; the rest of the arithmetic follows, and every x from 0 to 0.12 gives a maximal coupling. The maximal couplings of the example form a segment in the nine-dimensional polytope. That is the first of the two problems that Dzhafarov, Cervantes and Kujala (2017) name: the maximal coupling is not unique, so a verdict on a whole system may depend on which point of the segment one takes.

The second problem is about lumping. A noncontextual system can become contextual when some answers are merged, say fair with poor. If one wants a verdict that survives coarsening the question, the coarsenings have to be part of the definition. Their remedy is to describe a many-valued answer by its splits. A split is a dichotomization: choose a set W of values and record only whether the answer lies in W. For four answers there are 24−1−1=7 splits, since W and its complement give the same binary variable (Figure 13.1). With k answers there are 2k−1−1: 3, 7, 15, 31 for k=3,…,6. A binary variable has a unique maximal coupling, with Pr(both copies in W)=min{p(W),q(W)}, so each split gives one unambiguous requirement on the table r. A coupling meets a requirement when it lies on a certain face of the polytope. Asking several splits to be maximal at once asks the coupling to lie on the intersection of their faces, and an intersection of faces can be empty.

For the example, that is exactly what happens. The four one-value splits fix the diagonal at the ceiling, so we are on the segment above. The two-value split {1,2}∣{3,4} asks for Pr(both in {1,2})=min(0.50,0.46)=0.46. Already r11+r22=0.34, and r21=0 because row 2 has nothing off the diagonal to give, so r12=0.12: all of column 2’s remaining need must come from row 1. The split {1,4}∣{2,3} asks for min(0.50,0.50)=0.50, and the same reasoning gives r14=0.16: all of row 1’s spare mass must go to column 4. But row 1 has only 0.16 to give, and these two requirements ask for 0.12+0.16. No coupling meets all seven. A linear program over the polytope agrees: the best total agreement over the seven splits falls short of the sum of the seven bounds by 0.24 (a number from our own computation, in units of summed agreement probabilities). Each split alone is satisfiable and the seven together are not.

13.2All splits, and a stringent condition on the margins

Dzhafarov, Cervantes and Kujala (2017) solved this case in general. For two copies of one k-valued variable, requiring every split to be maximal reduces to the one-value and two-value splits (their Theorem 4.3), and the reduced system has a solution exactly when one of the two distributions nominally dominates the other. p nominally dominates q if pi<qi for at most one value i (Theorem 4.6). In words, at most one answer is more popular in q than in p; the other answers are all at least as popular in p.

Figure 13.2 shows two pairs. In the left pair the second distribution is the first after the invented warm-interviewer drift, applied to a five-answer version of p. Three answers gain and two lose, so neither survey’s margin nominally dominates the other. In the right pair one answer takes a large share and the others all give a little; dominance holds. Dominance is a statement about the sign pattern of p−q: it fails as soon as two values gain and two values lose. What dominance does allow is one answer becoming popular at everyone else’s expense, a little from each, or the reverse.

We checked that we had Theorem 4.6 right before leaning on it. For 900 random pairs of distributions, 300 each at k=3, 4 and 5, drawn uniformly from the simplex with a fixed seed, we solved the linear program that maximizes total agreement over all two-way splits and compared it with the sign count. The two agreed on all of them. That checks our coding of the statement, not the theorem, whose proof is in the paper’s supplement, which we have not read.

Dominance never fails for two or three answers. With two values there is one difference and it has one sign. With three, the differences sum to zero, and two gains with two losses would need four values. So for k≤3 two copies of one variable cannot be contextual by themselves, and a many-valued variable first behaves differently at k=4. For random margins the failure is common. Pairs drawn independently and uniformly from the simplex fail dominance 60 percent of the time at k=4, 85 percent at k=5 and 95 percent at k=6 (our seeded simulation, 20,000 pairs per k). Under the invented drift of the opening example, applied to random four-value distributions, cycle 9b found two thirds failing. The authors call the condition “stringent” and write that it is “likely to be violated in many empirical systems.” Their concluding remarks add that for two continuous distributions the condition fails whenever the densities differ: if one density is larger on one interval and smaller on another, take two subintervals of each, and any partition that contains all four breaks it.

Look at what that does to an investigator. Under all splits, a margin shift on a scale of four or more answers, which surveys with a different mode, wording or sample can easily show, can make the system contextual before any third table is consulted. The verdict is then about the margins and says nothing about whether the tables glue.

13.3Only the cuts

If the answers are ordered, merging fair with excellent while leaving good out is not a coarsening that anyone would propose. Kujala and Dzhafarov (2022) turn that intuition into a rule. Give the set of answers a notion of neighborhood, and call a split allowable when both of its parts are connected under it. For answers on a line the connected sets are the intervals, so the allowable splits are the cuts, {X≤l} against {X>l}, k−1 of them (the first three rows of Figure 13.1). For labels with no structure every split is allowable. Structure in between gives something in between: for their example of a dot that can appear in one of five positions arranged as a plus sign, 13 of the 15 splits are allowable. Allowable coarsenings compose, so a rule built on them keeps a noncontextual system noncontextual when answers are lumped.

With cuts, everything that went wrong above goes away. Let U be uniform on [0,1] and set X=Fp−1(U), X′=Fq−1(U), where F is the distribution function and F−1 its quantile function. This is the quantile coupling, the comonotone one that sends mass up the scale in step. At every cut l it gives Pr(X≤l,X′≤l)=min{Fp(l),Fq(l)}, the largest possible, so all cuts are maximal at once. That is Theorem 16 of the 2022 paper: a single connection split by cuts is never contextual by itself. In the example the quantile coupling is r11=.24, r12=.16, r22=.06, r23=.04, r33=.24, r34=.16, r44=.10, all other entries zero. It puts 0.64 on the diagonal, below the 0.72 that the four one-value splits demand. That is the price: the one-value splits {2} and {3} are not cuts and are no longer asked to be maximal.

The quantile coupling is one of many couplings that meet all the cuts. Theorem 17 says which. Look at one cut l. A coupling sends some mass across it upward, from X≤l to X′>l, and some downward. The net is fixed by the margins, because Pr(X≤l)=Pr(X≤l,X′≤l)+up and Pr(X′≤l)=Pr(X≤l,X′≤l)+down, so up−down=Fp(l)−Fq(l). Maximal agreement at this cut means that the smaller of the two crossing probabilities is zero. In the plane of the two copies, with copy X along one axis and copy X′ along the other, the cut divides the grid into four blocks, two where the copies sit on the same side and two where they straddle it. The block that crosses against the sign of Fp(l)−Fq(l) must be empty, and if Fp(l)=Fq(l) both straddling blocks must be (Figure 13.3, left). Collect the forbidden blocks over all cuts and call the union K. A coupling is admitted if and only if it puts no mass in K. The algebra of the previous paragraph is ours; the theorem is the paper’s, with its proof in the part of the paper we did read. As with Theorem 4.6, we checked our coding of the statement: on 1800 random couplings of random pairs, total agreement over the cuts reached its ceiling exactly when the coupling had no mass in K, and the quantile coupling never had any.

Figure 13.4 turns the same pair into mass over the grid. The quantile coupling has eight occupied cells, a staircase climbing through the unshaded region. The independent coupling p⊗q, which ignores the fact that the two copies are the same question, puts 0.595 of its mass on forbidden cells. Summed over the four cuts, the agreement probabilities reach their ceiling of 3.6 for the quantile coupling and fall to 2.41 for the independent one.

Which misreports the cut rule trusts

Now put a loop back. Suppose a population of (X,Y,Z) exists, surveys 1 and 3 report truthfully, and survey 2 reports a misreported X′ in place of X. The joint of the true X and the reported X′ is a coupling of the two copies of X, and all the other pairs of copies agree trivially. If that coupling puts no mass in K, the cut rule is satisfied, and it cannot raise a false alarm. This short argument is ours; it is how the project read Theorem 17.

So the rule trusts a misreport whose own coupling crosses each cut in one direction only. Upward drift qualifies. A pull toward the middle qualifies, because values below the middle cross cuts upward and values above cross downward but each cut is crossed one way. A push toward the extremes qualifies. Symmetric noise, one step up or one step down with equal chance, does not: it crosses each cut both ways. On the invented p of Figure 13.2(a) with 40 percent of respondents moving, the three admitted drifts put no mass in the forbidden region, and symmetric noise puts 0.08 there (our computation, same script). The all-splits rule trusts less. At three values it trusts only the misreports that change as few answers as the margins require, and the shift up the scale is not among them. At four or more values the margins alone must also pass nominal dominance, and even the pull toward the middle fails it (see the cycle 10 table below).

One more observation. Choosing the splits is choosing which coarse-grainings of the answers the glue must respect. In the language of Part I that is a statement about which restriction maps the gluing has to commute with. Neither paper says it that way, and we have not worked out whether it connects to sheaves with non-identity restriction maps; we note it because the authors themselves contrast their treatment with Abramsky’s.

13.4What the papers say

What the paper says: Dzhafarov, Cervantes and Kujala (2017), “Contextuality in canonical systems of random variables”

The paper starts from the two problems above, non-unique maximal couplings and instability under lumping, and answers both by representing every measurement through its binary splits and asking each split’s copies to be coupled maximally; for several copies, “multimaximally.” A k-valued answer always receives its k one-value splits, and which coarser splits to add is left to the analyst. Section 4 takes two copies of one variable with all splits, proves that only one- and two-value splits matter, and characterizes the noncontextual case by nominal dominance. The concluding remarks carry the stringency remark quoted above, note that for ordered values it “may be natural” to allow only runs of successive values, with cuts as a stronger restriction, and say that developing restricted splits is future work. We read Sections 1 to 5; the proofs in the supplement we did not read. Its analysis of all splits is about a single connection of two copies. It has no data and does not say what nominal dominance does to a loop of surveys.

What the paper says: Kujala and Dzhafarov (2022), “Contextuality and dichotomizations of random variables”

This is the follow-up on restricted splits. It states principles that a notion of contextuality should meet, among them that a noncontextual system stays noncontextual under coarse-graining, derives the allowable splits from the neighborhood structure of the values, and for ordered values arrives at cuts. Theorem 16 gives the quantile coupling and Theorem 17 the set of admitted couplings. For unordered labels it returns to nominal dominance (Theorem 19) and shows that for three or more copies dominance is necessary but not sufficient (Example 20). For values in a region of Rn it has no approach it finds satisfactory beyond treating the coordinates separately. We read Sections 1 and 4 to 8; Sections 2 and 3, which hold the formal definitions and the principle of Analyticity, we did not. The sections we read do not discuss misreporting mechanisms, loops of surveys or sampling, and the sentence “a misreport is trusted if it crosses each cut one way” is the project’s reading of Theorem 17, not the authors’. It follows, though the sections we read do not make a point of it, that the ordering is supplied by the analyst: a five-point agreement scale treated as ordered or as five labels admits different couplings and can give different verdicts on the same tables.

Two things from the earlier chapters bear on both papers. Kujala, Dzhafarov and Larsson (2015), met in Chapter 11, give the criterion for yes-or-no variables, which these papers extend. The 2017 paper’s Example 3.1 notes that maximal couplings of single variables ignore the joint distributions within each survey, and that in the approach of Abramsky and colleagues (Chapter 9) this is “never acceptable”; the joined variable must then be added to the system. Our experiments follow the by-default side and do not add it.

13.5What we found

Cycle 9: three values

Cycle 9 ran before we had read either paper. Cycle 8 had found contextuality-by-default quiet under one-way misreports of a yes-or-no variable, and we suspected that this was a fact about two values. With three there is no closed form, so we computed the verdict from its definition: a linear program over the 729 joint outcomes of the six survey-specific copies that maximizes how often the copies of each variable agree, subject to the three tables. The shortfall from the largest agreement the margins allow is positive exactly when the system is contextual. Two checks. For two values the program reproduced the closed-form criterion on all 3,000 table sets, a quarter of them (24.4 percent) contextual, with the shortfall equal to half the closed form’s excess to within 10−11. And on the invented tables X=Y, Y=Z, X≠Z at three values, which cannot glue, it returned a shortfall of 1.

One population always exists behind the tables, and survey 2 misreports X in five ways, each applied with probability s=0.1 and, separately, s=0.4: single-step (0 reported as 1), to-middle (0 or 2 reported as 1), shift-up (0 as 1 and 1 as 2), single-step on Z (0 as 1 only when Z=2) and assimilate as in cycle 8. The table gives, at s=0.4, the share of 2,000 random populations called incoherent, counting only violations larger than 0.01; “diffuse” and “concentrated” are Dirichlet draws with weights 1 and 0.2. The third column is the share of answers the mechanism changes divided by the least any misreport must change to produce the same shift in the margin (median over populations).

Populations Mechanism Changed / required By-default Pooling
Diffuse single-step 1.0 0 1.0%
Diffuse to-middle 1.0 0 2.2%
Diffuse shift-up 1.7 0 0.9%
Diffuse assimilate 4.7 2.7% 8.3%
Concentrated single-step 1.0 0 50.5%
Concentrated to-middle 1.0 0 74.4%
Concentrated single-step on Z 1.0 0 22.8%
Concentrated shift-up 1.5 7.0% 67.3%
Concentrated assimilate 2.1 43.8% 86.8%

The by-default criterion raised no false alarm, of any size, in the 24,000 populations (both values of s) where that ratio is one, and raised them only where it exceeds one. The condition is elementary. Every respondent who moves leaves one value and enters another, so the number moved is at least half the sum, over values, of the absolute net change in the margin, with equality exactly when no value both gains and loses respondents. With two values that is “one way”, which is what cycle 8 found. With three it is not: to-middle has two sources and one sink and is safe, while shift-up runs in one direction but the middle value gains from below and loses upward. And shift-up does not depend on Y or Z. In cycle 7 that independence made the criterion right by construction, and that was a fact about two values. On an ordered scale shift-up is the plainest description of a survey that draws slightly higher answers, and the criterion false-alarms on it. Cycle 8’s “one-way” rule was a special case. It would be surprising if this two-line algebra were new to anyone who works on couplings.

Reading the 2017 paper afterwards confirmed the program and changed how we read it. For three values the splits are one value against the rest, which is what the program imposes, so our derivation had been right and cycle 9 had run the all-splits version without our knowing it by that name. Because dominance never fails at three values, a connection of two copies cannot be contextual by itself there; the false alarms above come through the loop. At four values it can, and the same drift on random four-value margins, 20,000 of them, failed dominance for 67.2 percent in diffuse populations and 66.2 percent in concentrated ones.

Cycle 9b: cuts only

The 2017 paper suggests cuts for ordered values, so experiment 9b imposed maximal agreement on the cuts alone, on three-value populations drawn the same way (2,000 per cell, s=0.4; each cell shows the share flagged with any violation, then with violations above 0.01). The first run failed on a missing __file__ when importing experiment 9’s definitions; the fix touched no numbers.

Populations Mechanism All splits Cuts
Concentrated shift-up 9.3% / 6.4% 0 / 0
Concentrated assimilate 56.1% / 41.4% 47.6% / 33.4%
Diffuse assimilate 5.5% / 3.5% 4.2% / 2.3%
Either single-step, to-middle, single-step on Z 0 0

Shift-up raised no false alarm in 4,000 populations with cuts. The reason is the one in the previous section: the reported answer X′ is never below the true X, so Pr(X≤l,X′≤l)=Pr(X′≤l), the smaller of the two distribution functions. Assimilation still false-alarms, because it moves answers toward Z in both directions, and the effect of a context on an association survives both rules. The set of admitted splits is one more comparison rule, after pooling against coupling and maximal against other couplings. (The all-splits rates differ slightly from experiment 9’s because the seed changed.)

Cycle 10: four and five ordered values

Cycle 10 came after reading Kujala and Dzhafarov (2022). It uses four and five ordered values and six misreports of X in survey 2, each moving an answer one step with probability 0.4 (and, for four values, also 0.1): shift-up, to-middle, to-extremes, shift-up on Z (only when Z is above the middle), noise (up or down with equal chance) and assimilate (toward Z). A population always exists, so every flag is a false alarm. Share of concentrated populations flagged at s=0.4, violations above 0.01, with 600 populations per cell for four values and 200 for five:

Four values Five values
Mechanism Cuts All splits Pooling Cuts All splits Pooling
shift-up 0 65.8% 45.0% 0 86.5% 14.0%
to-middle 0 100% 50.2% 0 77.0% 27.0%
to-extremes 0 100% 54.5% 0 100% 23.0%
shift-up on Z 0 60.2% 27.8% 0 86.5% 2.0%
noise 1.2% 57.2% 15.5% 0 87.5% 1.5%
assimilate 8.5% 69.7% 48.8% 3.0% 88.5% 15.5%

With cuts, the four mechanisms that Theorem 17 admits raised no false alarm of any size in 11,200 populations (the notebook says 28 cells; the results file has 24, which is what 11,200 adds up to). Noise and assimilation raised a few, none in diffuse populations. With all splits the verdict is usually “contextual”, and almost all of that is the margins alone: for shift-up at four values the margins-alone verdict, nominal dominance, is 67.8 percent against 70.8 percent for all splits with any violation. The loop did not have to be consulted. And the cut rule has not gone blind. On tables with equal margins and a real contradiction, two pairs associated one way and the third reversed, given weight w against uniform noise, all three verdicts were zero at w=0.2 and positive at w=0.4, for four values and for five.

Three cautions went with this. The apparent trend of false alarms falling as the number of values rises, for noise and assimilation, is confounded: a Dirichlet draw over 27, 64 and 125 outcomes is a different population each time, and pooling’s rate falls too. A zero in a five-value cell with 200 populations means under about 1.5 percent, not zero; the one-way cells are zero by the theorem, not by the count. And the result says nothing about power when margins differ. That last point set the next cycle.

Cycle 11: what the cut rule misses

The cut rule is quiet, and we asked whether that is because it admits too much. Here no population exists, because the three tables do not glue, and on top of that survey 2 misreports X by a mechanism the cut rule admits. The right verdict is “incoherent” every time.

On random four-value systems we replaced the (Y,Z) table by a mixture, with weight w, of itself and the most reversed table with the same margins, and kept the systems that failed to glue by more than 0.01 before any misreport. The table gives the share of those still flagged by the cut rule afterwards (any shortfall above 10−7):

Shift-up To-middle
Populations w Incoherent s=0.1 s=0.4 s=0.1 s=0.4
Diffuse 0.6 41 of 600 24% 2% 51% 24%
Concentrated 0.3 175 of 600 43% 8% 73% 34%
Concentrated 0.6 476 of 600 79% 30% 93% 65%

Diffuse systems at w=0.3 produced none that were incoherent. (The memo printed 31 percent in the last row’s shift-up cell at s=0.4 until November 14, when it was corrected to 30.5; the results file has 0.3046, so 30 is the rounding.) Figure 13.5 draws the same numbers. A ten percent upward drift hides between a fifth and three quarters of the incoherent systems, and a forty percent drift hides between two thirds and nearly all. The median system keeps none of its shortfall after shift-up at s=0.4, in every row. Counting only shortfalls above 0.01 the retention is lower still: after shift-up at s=0.4, 2, 4 and 21 percent in the three rows. Pooling flags more of these systems, 12 to 89 percent, but cycle 10 showed that it also flags often when nothing is wrong, so its flags cannot be read.

A strong, symmetric contradiction survives. With uniform margins, two pairs associated with weight w and the third reversed, the cut rule and pooling both begin to flag at w=0.34 for four values and 0.38 for five, on a grid of 0.02. (The memo said “every verdict” until November 14; the all-splits verdict was not located on that grid.) With an admitted misreport the cut rule’s threshold moves from 0.34 to at most 0.44 for four values (shift-up, s=0.4) and from 0.38 to at most 0.46 for five (to-middle, s=0.4); to-extremes and shift-up on Z do not move it. Weak or lopsided contradictions, which is what random systems mostly are, do not survive.

Read this against the definition and it is unsurprising: the rule asks whether any admitted coupling explains the tables, and a gap between margins enlarges the set of admitted couplings. The numbers size the effect; they did not discover it. They carry three limits. The incoherent systems were built one way, by pushing a single table toward reversal, and the retention rates depend on that and on the 0.01 cutoff. Many of the systems are only slightly incoherent, and the diffuse row rests on 41 of them. And everything is population tables, the random systems at four values only; sampling enters in Chapters 14 to 16.

The cycle’s moral is cycle 7’s, now on ordered scales. The cautious verdict errs toward silence, pooling errs toward alarm, and the size of each error is set by how far the shared margins have moved. What would help is a bound that relates the margin gap to the incoherence it can hide, and that is Chapter 14. Nothing in these cycles was established as new. Each piece is a case of a result in the two papers or an elementary consequence of one; what the cycles add is the sizes, in these designs.

Try it

Try it 13.1. Show that for three answer categories one of any two distributions nominally dominates the other. Then give two four-value distributions that fail dominance, and say which two splits of the opening example’s argument collide for the pair.

Try it 13.2. Take the invented p and q of the opening. Work out the quantile coupling by hand and check that it matches the entries in the text, that it meets all three cuts, and that it falls short of the one-value split {2}. What is its total agreement, and how does it compare with the ceiling 0.72?

Try it 13.3. Four answers sit on a ring, 1–2–3–4–1, and a part is allowed when it is connected through neighbors around the ring. Which of the seven splits of Figure 13.1 are allowable? Compare with the cuts of a line. (This applies the connectedness rule as we understand it from the paper’s example of the five-position dot; check that it is the rule wanted.)

Try it 13.4. Prove that up−down=Fp(l)−Fq(l) at each cut, and use it to show that a coupling is admitted at cut l if and only if at most one of the two crossing probabilities is positive. Then compute the coupling that a symmetric noise misreport makes of p=(.4,.1,.4,.1) at s=0.4 and find its mass in K.

Try it 13.5. In Figure 13.3, set two ordered distributions, or reset to its invented pair, and read off whether all splits and whether cuts are satisfied. Then let the second distribution be the first after a drift mechanism and watch the mass in the forbidden region: it stays zero for shift-up, to-middle and to-extremes, and becomes positive for noise.
